entities.summary:
Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480 – 524 or 525 CE) was a Roman senator, consul, and Christian philosopher who served as *magister officiorum* under Theodoric the Great during the twilight of the Western Roman Empire and the nascent Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy. His life and tragic death encapsulate the profound intellectual and political transitions of the early 6th century, bridging classical antiquity with the medieval period through his monumental project to translate and reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian thought. Operating from Rome, his work profoundly shaped the curriculum and philosophical discourse of the coming millennium.

Boethius's intellectual ambition was vast: to translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin and demonstrate their underlying harmony, a project intended to preserve Greek thought for a Latin-speaking world. Though unfinished, his translations of Aristotle's logical works (the *Organon*) became the foundational texts for logic in Western Europe for centuries, known as the *Logica vetus*. His original treatises on arithmetic (*De institutione arithmetica*), music (*De institutione musica*), and geometry, based on Greek sources, established the *quadrivium* as a core component of medieval education. His most famous work, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, written while imprisoned under suspicion of treason, is a dialogue between Boethius and Lady Philosophy, exploring fate, free will, evil, and the nature of happiness.
